comment_text: I am a 70 year old retired U.S. Army Master Sergeant (E8/1972-1993) and former defense contractor worker bee (2005-2010) who spent much of his career in the cold war. What we currently have in Ukraine is similar to the situation that existed for most of WWI on the west front: a stalemate with small gains won or lost by either side from day-to-day. Ukraine simply does not have enough equipment, forces or resources to take back the land they lost in 2022. On the flip side Russia no longer possesses the conventional forces needed to win the war on their terms as long as NATO nations continue to provide equipment and supplies to Ukraine. As for the lost land, Ukraine must accept the ground reality that the land they have lost to Russia is gone forever, especially the Crimea. The only way that could ever change would be if NATO directly intervenes in the war and fights Russia. If that were to happen, we would quickly move to WWIII and most likely a large nuclear exchange, so realistically I don't see such NATO intervention happening, as the stakes are just too high. The question at this point is how much more destruction and death must occur before both sides finally accept the truth that the current situation on the ground is as good as it going to get, and both sides finally end the war?  While personally I don't like to see Russia end the war with Ukrainian land as their ill-gotten gains, the war with it's ever increasing death and destruction must end before it at some point spirals further out of control and we end up in WWIII.

Zelenskyy is not able to cede Crimea, or any other part of Ukraine to Russia. 
 
Under Ukraine’s current constitution, Crimea cannot be legally ceded to Russia without a very difficult process.

Here’s why:
	•	Territorial Integrity: The Constitution of Ukraine (1996) states clearly in Article 2 that “The territory of Ukraine within its present borders is indivisible and inviolable.” Crimea is internationally recognized as part of Ukraine’s territory, despite Russia’s 2014 annexation.
	•	Amending the Constitution: To legally change the borders of Ukraine (such as ceding Crimea), Article 73 of the Constitution requires an all-Ukrainian referendum — meaning the entire population of Ukraine would have to vote on it, not just Crimea or a government decision alone.
	•	Procedure for Amendments: Constitutional amendments involving territorial issues are also subject to a complex process under Articles 154–159. Any change would need:
	•	A proposal by the President or at least one-third of the Parliament (Verkhovna Rada),
	•	Approval by a constitutional majority (at least 300 out of 450 deputies) in Parliament,
	•	And possibly review by the Constitutional Court to ensure the amendment fits within the framework of constitutional principles.
	•	Practical Reality: Politically and socially, the overwhelming majority of Ukrainian politicians and the public view Crimea as an integral part of Ukraine. Thus, even starting the legal process to cede it would likely be impossible under current conditions.

Summary:
Legally, Ukraine would need a national referendum and constitutional amendment to cede Crimea — both extremely unlikely. As it stands, the Ukrainian Constitution protects the country’s territorial integrity very strongly.

Core Takeaway
To this day, Ukrainians have fought with extreme determination, especially in urban warfare.
However, in every battle where Russia fully committed its forces and followed through,
Russia ultimately emerged victorious — often at high cost, but with ground gained.

⚔ Battle Summaries
1. Kiev (Feb–Apr 2022)

Russia launched an assault but never fully committed to siege or urban warfare.

Withdrew under logistical strain and in light of Istanbul peace talks.

No full commitment — Ukrainian defensive success.

2. Kharkiv (Feb–Sep 2022)

Russia occupied areas around Kharkiv but avoided full urban battle.

Ukrainian counteroffensive reclaimed territory; Russian troops withdrew without fight.

No committed battle — Ukrainian gain by maneuver.

3. Mariupol (Feb–May 2022)

Full Russian commitment with siege tactics; total encirclement.

Ukrainians (especially Azov) resisted heroically for months.

Result: Russian victory. City was taken after brutal fighting.

4. Severodonetsk (May–Jun 2022)

Russia committed to grinding urban battle, block-by-block assault.

Ukrainians fought hard but made a tactical withdrawal.

Result: Russian victory.

5. Bakhmut (Aug 2022–May 2023)

Months-long meat-grinder; Ukrainians fought fiercely, trench by trench.

Wagner-led Russian forces fully committed and took the city.

Result: Russian victory. Most symbolic and bloody fight.

6. Avdiivka (Late 2023–Feb 2024)

Russia launched major offensive with full artillery, drone, and infantry use.

Ukraine resisted over months but finally withdrew to avoid encirclement.

Result: Russian victory.
Conclusion:
Ukraine: unmatched bravery, held key symbolic ground early on.

Russia: won every major battle where it chose to fully commit and endure.

These victories, though costly, show Russian superiority in protracted ground engagements — once it decides to finish what it starts.

comment_text: The Spartan series of AFVs had to be small and lightweight because it is airmobile. In other words, can be carried in aircraft. The aircraft it was designed to be carried in was the C130 Hercules. The spartan only weighs about ten tonnes, so a Hercules could carry two of them. The idea was to provide some armour for airmobile forces but it had to sacrifice armoured protection, which is, of course, heavy, and to substitute protection with speed and mobility in a quick deployment. comment_text: @@Bravo_Two_Zero  A lot of people make comments about them without knowing what they're talking about. True the armour isn't up to modern western standards but it's about as good a base model  BMP. Almost all maintenance and repairs with the exception of lifting the engine and gearbox can be done with onboard tools even the engine decks can be lifted off by hand it just takes four men and the right coordination. The engine is a standard Cummins diesel so it and the gearbox can be lifted out with any basic vehicle mounted crane or even a good chain hoist. It's not a Bradley a Warrior or a BMP it's never going to go toe to toe with enemy armour because that's not the job it was built for but it is a cheap fast reliable battlefield taxi able to get infantry anti armour or anti air teams into ambush positions quickly and quietly through terrain no other vehicles could. That's why the troop capacity is so small it was never supposed to carry a section of regular infantry it was designed to move small teams of specialists to wherever they were needed most quickly to size and defend critical objectives until slower heavier elements could arrive. Such as airfield's power plants bridges ect. It was designed post WWII when the British forces were drawing down and maintaining large garrison's in all our remaining overseas territories simply wasn't affordable so we switched to a large airmobile rapid response force which could secure a beach head for larger forces to use.

The vast majority of Americans continue to support Ukraine. We believe that it is the right thing to do. I think it's worth addressing Trump saying that Ukraine has been "taking advantage of" American aid: in one sense, that's true, I don't think that, even in victory, Ukraine is likely to be able to repay America financially, because Russia's brutality has caused billions of dollars worth of damage, and Ukraine will need to worry about rebuilding. However, we knew from the start that this wasn't about getting paid back, it's just the right thing to do. Zelensky's repeated thanks for American aid demonstrate that he understands this, too, that this is just one group of people helping another. And in recent polls, over 70% of Americans still think that this is worth doing, with over half saying that they believe that we should aid for as long as it takes, until Ukraine is restored to pre-invasion borders. With those numbers, it's clear that even those who voted for Trump did so for other reasons. So I want our Ukrainian friends to know... the majority of Americans, we still support you, even if it might not seem like it when you hear Trump.

But I also want to say: Even though we don't expect to be repaid and we want to support Ukraine because it's the right thing to do, many are simply unaware of the other ways that Ukraine is repaying us for our help. Ukrainian soldiers have experience that nobody else in the world has, and they've already begun to pass their knowledge on to NATO countries, including the US. I want to say thank you to Ukraine for this effort. Thank you for helping to train Americans so that they are more prepared in case another war breaks out.

I am so sorry for Trump's betrayal. I understand that he might stop aid again, and no matter how supportive I feel, that doesn't translate into 155 mm artillery shells, I don't have the ability to give the aid that my country's government can. I'll be praying for you, because that's what I can do, and pushing in the tiny way I can to ensure support continues, because I can do that, too.

The U.S. does not currently have any systems quite like Archer or Caesar. In fact, the U.S. Army has recognized the need for wheeled self-propelled artillery, which is why it is currently testing the BAE Systems Archer and the French Caesar as potential future acquisitions.

The closest systems in the U.S. arsenal are: HIMARS (High Mobility Artillery Rocket System); M109A7 Paladin (Tracked Self-Propelled Howitzer). However, neither is a true equivalent.

HIMARS offers similar mobility but is well-suited for a different role. HIMARS offers comparable high mobility, but it is far more expensive, logistically demanding, and not suited for the same tactical role as Archer and Caesar. HIMARS excels at striking high-value, distant targets with precision-guided rockets and ballistic missiles, but it lacks the sustained firepower needed for frequent engagements against platoon- or squad-sized elements—a role for which Archer and Caesar are much better suited.


Attempting to use HIMARS in this way would be cost-prohibitive, both in terms of munitions and operational overhead. Not to mention that the cost per launcher and per munition is roughly 10 times higher than traditional 155mm artillery shells.
M109A7 Paladin: Heavily Armored but Less Mobile

The M109A7 Paladin is more similar to Archer and Caesar in terms of function, but it is: More expensive; Heavier and slower; Less mobile in dynamic battlefield conditions; Slower rate of fire. The tracked Paladin is optimized for sustained operations in a high-intensity conflict—the kind of large-scale armor engagements envisioned during the Cold War. It was designed to support heavy mechanized formations in battles between armored brigades, rather than the highly mobile shoot-and-scoot doctrine seen in modern warfare.

Archer and Caesar are superior for the type of modern artillery warfare seen in Ukraine, where:

Mobility and evasion are more important than survivability in direct combat
Firepower needs to be sustained yet cost-effective
Rapid deployment & relocation ("shoot-and-scoot") is critical to avoid counterbattery fire

While the Paladin offers greater armor protection, it is ill-suited for fast-moving, cost-sensitive conflicts where a well-timed artillery barrage followed by immediate relocation is the key to survival. In contrast, Archer and Caesar’s wheeled platforms allow for quick repositioning and lower logistical costs, making them far more practical in modern asymmetrical warfare.

Russia also does not have a direct equivalent to the Archer or Caesar wheeled self-propelled howitzers in terms of mobility, automation, and modern battlefield effectiveness. While Russia fields a variety of self-propelled artillery systems, most are either tracked (like the M109A7 Paladin) or less advanced in automation and mobility than Archer and Caesar.

Former President of Poland Lech Walesa wrote the following letter to Trump.
Your Excellency, Mr. President,
We watched the report of your conversation with the President of Ukraine, Volodymyr Zelensky, with fear and distaste. We find it insulting that you expect Ukraine to show respect and gratitude for the material assistance provided by the United States in its fight against russia. Gratitude is owed to the heroic Ukrainian soldiers who shed their blood in defense of the values of the free world. They have been dying on the front lines for more than 11 years in the name of these values and the independence of their homeland, which was attacked by Putin’s russia.
We do not understand how the leader of a country that symbolizes the free world cannot recognize this.
Our alarm was also heightened by the atmosphere in the Oval Office during this conversation, which reminded us of the interrogations we endured at the hands of the Security Services and the debates in Communist courts. Prosecutors and judges, acting on behalf of the all-powerful communist political police, would explain to us that they held all the power while we held none. They demanded that we cease our activities, arguing that thousands of innocent people suffered because of us. They stripped us of our freedoms and civil rights because we refused to cooperate with the government or express gratitude for our oppression. We are shocked that President Volodymyr Zelensky was treated in the same manner.
The history of the 20th century shows that whenever the United States sought to distance itself from democratic values and its European allies, it ultimately became a threat to itself. President Woodrow Wilson understood this when he decided in 1917 that the United States must join World War I. President Franklin Delano Roosevelt understood this when, after the attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941, he resolved that the war to defend America must be fought not only in the Pacific but also in Europe, in alliance with the nations under attack by the Third Reich.
We remember that without President Ronald Reagan and America’s financial commitment, the collapse of the Soviet empire would not have been possible. President Reagan recognized that millions of enslaved people suffered in Soviet russia and the countries it had subjugated, including thousands of political prisoners who paid for their defense of democratic values with their freedom. His greatness lay, among other things, in his unwavering decision to call the USSR an “Empire of Evil” and to fight it decisively. We won, and today, the statue of President Ronald Reagan stands in Warsaw, facing the U.S. Embassy.
Mr. President, material aid—military and financial—can never be equated with the blood shed in the name of Ukraine’s independence and the freedom of Europe and the entire free world. Human life is priceless; its value cannot be measured in money. Gratitude is due to those who sacrifice their blood and their freedom. This is self-evident to us, the people of Solidarity, former political prisoners of the communist regime under Soviet russia.
We call on the United States to uphold the guarantees made alongside Great Britain in the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, which established a direct obligation to defend Ukraine’s territorial integrity in exchange for its relinquishment of nuclear weapons. These guarantees are unconditional—there is no mention of treating such assistance as an economic transaction.
Signed,
Lech Wałęsa, former political prisoner, President of Poland
